BIN381 Milestone 3 - Modelling, Evaluation and Deployment

Group P1: Alexander Solomon (Person A), Rudi Jan du Plessis (Person B), Timothy Wubbeling (Person C)

2026-10-05

This notebook runs the whole of Milestone 3 end to end from a clean R session, in the order the work was handed over:

  • Part A - Modelling strategy and implementation (Task 1). Starts from the Milestone 2 train/test split in data/integrated/, tunes and fits the candidate models, and writes them with their predictions to data/modelling/.
  • Part B - Evaluation and interpretation (Tasks 2 and 3). Evaluates Part A’s models without refitting them, selects the final model and threshold, and writes the evaluation outputs to data/evaluation/.
  • Part C - Deployment, monitoring and ethics (Task 4 and the ethics part of Task 3). Checks that the Shiny app in app/ serves the selected model, validates new data and reproduces Part B’s results exactly, and sets the fairness and monitoring evidence.

Each part is also a standalone notebook in notebook/; this file includes them unchanged as child documents. Packages are pinned in renv.lock (run renv::restore() first).

Part A - Modelling Strategy and Implementation (Alexander Solomon)

This notebook covers Task 1: modelling strategy and implementation. It starts from Milestone 2’s validated data set and train/test split and does not redo cleaning, integration or feature engineering. Three candidate classifiers are built in a tidymodels workflow, tuned with stratified cross-validation on the training set, and handed off: predictions to Person B (Rudi, Task 2/3) and fitted workflows plus an input schema to Person C (Timothy, Task 4).

1.1 Analytical Question and Task Type

This is a multi-class classification problem: Business Objective 2 asks for households to be classified into food-insecurity vulnerability tiers. The target is Vulnerability_Tier (Food secure / Food insecure / Severely food insecure), derived in Milestone 2 from FI_Score on 20,925 households. Food_Insecure_Binary is kept as a fallback in case the thin middle tier (10.55% of households) is hard to separate, but the 3-tier target is primary.

1.2 Load the Milestone 2 Split

The train/test split is not re-created here. Milestone 2 already produced a stratified 70/30 split (seed = 381) on the validated, leakage-checked data set, so M2_train.rds and M2_test.rds are loaded as-is rather than re-split.

train_raw <- readRDS(file.path(IN_DIR, "M2_train.rds"))
test_raw  <- readRDS(file.path(IN_DIR, "M2_test.rds"))

cat("Train:", nrow(train_raw), " Test:", nrow(test_raw),
    " Total:", nrow(train_raw) + nrow(test_raw), "\n")
## Train: 14646  Test: 6279  Total: 20925
stopifnot(nrow(train_raw) + nrow(test_raw) == 20925)

Leakage check

train_raw is Milestone 2’s full integrated file (128 columns), so the raw food-insecurity survey items are still present at this point - that’s expected. leakage_vars lists everything that must never reach the model; the actual check happens in 1.3, once predictors are selected.

leakage_vars <- c(
  "WorriedFoodWouldRunOutCode", "UnableToEatHealthyFoodCode", "AteFewFoodsCode",
  "SkippedMealCode", "AteLessCode", "RanOutOfFoodCode", "HungryButDidNotEatCode",
  "WholeDayWithoutEatingCode", "AdultHungerCode", "ChildHungerCode",
  "FewFoodsDays", "SkippedMealDays", "AteLessDays", "RanOutDays",
  "FI_Score", "n_fi_answered"
)

cat(ncol(train_raw), "columns loaded; leakage check runs once predictors are selected in 1.3.\n")
## 128 columns loaded; leakage check runs once predictors are selected in 1.3.

1.3 Predictor Set

The eight predictors are already engineered in Milestone 2 and reused as-is (Income_Log is log1p()-transformed income, Income_PerCapita is income divided by household size).

predictor_vars <- c("ComparativeIncomeCode", "GeoTypeCode", "HouseholdSize",
                    "Income_Log", "Income_PerCapita", "ElectricityAccessCode",
                    "SocialGrantRecipients", "MainToiletCode")
stopifnot(all(predictor_vars %in% names(train_raw)))
stopifnot(length(intersect(predictor_vars, leakage_vars)) == 0)  # predictor list is leakage-free

# Relabel tier levels to underscores so tidymodels' .pred_<level> columns don't contain spaces.
tier_lookup <- tibble(
  level = c("Food_secure", "Food_insecure", "Severely_food_insecure"),
  label = c("Food secure", "Food insecure", "Severely food insecure")
)

prep_df <- function(df) {
  df %>%
    mutate(
      Vulnerability_Tier = factor(Vulnerability_Tier, 
                                  levels = tier_lookup$label, 
                                  labels = tier_lookup$level),
      Food_Insecure_Binary = factor(Food_Insecure_Binary, 
                                    levels = c("Secure", "Insecure")),
      ComparativeIncomeCode = factor(ComparativeIncomeCode, 
                                     levels = 1:5, 
                                     ordered = TRUE),
      GeoTypeCode = factor(GeoTypeCode, 
                           levels = 1:3, 
                           labels = c("Urban", "Traditional_Tribal", "Farms")),
      ElectricityAccessCode = factor(ElectricityAccessCode, 
                                     levels = c(1, 2),
                                     labels = c("Yes", "No")),
      MainToiletCode = factor(MainToiletCode)
    ) %>%
    select(HouseholdID, Vulnerability_Tier, Food_Insecure_Binary, all_of(predictor_vars))
}

train <- prep_df(train_raw)
test  <- prep_df(test_raw)

present_leaks <- intersect(leakage_vars, names(train))
stopifnot(length(present_leaks) == 0)  # final predictor set is leakage-free

cat("Train class counts:\n"); print(table(train$Vulnerability_Tier))
## Train class counts:
## 
##            Food_secure          Food_insecure Severely_food_insecure 
##                  10172                   1545                   2929
cat("\nGeoTypeCode is 3 levels (Urban / Traditional-Tribal / Farms), corrected from the binary\n", 
    "urban/rural split Milestone 2's original encoding table assumed.\n")
## 
## GeoTypeCode is 3 levels (Urban / Traditional-Tribal / Farms), corrected from the binary
##  urban/rural split Milestone 2's original encoding table assumed.

1.4 Candidate Approaches and Assumptions

Three techniques, per the brief’s requirement for at least two defensible candidates:

  1. Regularised multinomial logistic regression (glmnet) - the interpretable baseline. Assumes linearity in the log-odds; Income_Log already addresses the raw-income skew that would otherwise violate this. A VIF-style check below looks at redundancy between ComparativeIncomeCode and the two income features, since all three relate to household income.
  2. Decision tree (rpart) - gives directly readable rules for the interpretability discussion, at the cost of instability. Treated as an interpretability option, not the performance candidate.
  3. Random forest (ranger) - the performance benchmark. No scaling or dummy-encoding needed for tree-based models.
vif_check <- train %>%
  mutate(CompIncomeNum = as.numeric(ComparativeIncomeCode)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(CompIncomeNum), !is.na(Income_Log), !is.na(Income_PerCapita))

m <- lm(CompIncomeNum ~ Income_Log + Income_PerCapita, data = vif_check)
r2 <- summary(m)$r.squared

cat("R-squared of ComparativeIncomeCode on the two income features:", 
    round(r2, 3), "\n")
## R-squared of ComparativeIncomeCode on the two income features: 0.064
cat("VIF-equivalent (1 / (1 - R2)):", 
    round(1 / (1 - r2), 2), "\n")
## VIF-equivalent (1 / (1 - R2)): 1.07
# VIF above ~5 is the usual threshold of concern

1.5 Recipes

Linear models need dummy-encoded, normalised predictors; tree-based models handle factors and unscaled numerics natively, so each gets its own recipe.

rec_linear <- recipe(Vulnerability_Tier ~ ., data = train %>% select(-HouseholdID, -Food_Insecure_Binary)) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_other(MainToiletCode, threshold = 0.02) %>%
  step_novel(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

rec_tree <- recipe(Vulnerability_Tier ~ ., data = train %>% select(-HouseholdID, -Food_Insecure_Binary)) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_other(MainToiletCode, threshold = 0.02) %>%
  step_novel(all_nominal_predictors())

1.6 Model Specifications

spec_logistic <- multinom_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = tune()) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

spec_tree <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = tune(), tree_depth = tune(), min_n = tune()) %>%
  set_engine("rpart") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

spec_forest <- rand_forest(mtry = tune(), min_n = tune(), trees = 500) %>%
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "permutation") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

wf_logistic <- workflow() %>% add_recipe(rec_linear) %>% add_model(spec_logistic)
wf_tree     <- workflow() %>% add_recipe(rec_tree)   %>% add_model(spec_tree)
wf_forest   <- workflow() %>% add_recipe(rec_tree)   %>% add_model(spec_forest)

1.7 Stratified Cross-Validation and Class Imbalance

Stratified k-fold CV keeps each fold’s class mix close to the training set’s 69.45/10.55/20.00 split. Class weighting is compared against plain stratification below to assess imbalance directly, rather than just noting it.

set.seed(381)
folds <- vfold_cv(train, v = 5, strata = Vulnerability_Tier)
print(folds)
## #  5-fold cross-validation using stratification 
## # A tibble: 5 × 2
##   splits               id   
##   <list>               <chr>
## 1 <split [11716/2930]> Fold1
## 2 <split [11716/2930]> Fold2
## 3 <split [11717/2929]> Fold3
## 4 <split [11717/2929]> Fold4
## 5 <split [11718/2928]> Fold5
# Frequency-inverse class weights, for comparison against unweighted stratified CV.
class_weights <- train %>%
  count(Vulnerability_Tier) %>%
  mutate(weight = sum(n) / (n_distinct(Vulnerability_Tier) * n))
print(class_weights)
##       Vulnerability_Tier     n    weight
## 1            Food_secure 10172 0.4799449
## 2          Food_insecure  1545 3.1598706
## 3 Severely_food_insecure  2929 1.6667805

1.8 Tuning

Tuning grids use space-filling designs (10-15 candidates per model) to keep the 5-fold search within reasonable runtime.

grid_logistic <- grid_space_filling(penalty(), mixture(), size = 12)
grid_tree <- grid_space_filling(cost_complexity(), tree_depth(), min_n(), size = 12)
grid_forest <- grid_space_filling(mtry(range = c(2, 8)), min_n(), size = 10)

metrics_tune <- metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy, bal_accuracy)
set.seed(381)
tuned_logistic <- tune_grid(
  wf_logistic, resamples = folds, grid = grid_logistic,
  metrics = metrics_tune, control = control_grid(save_pred = TRUE)
)
show_best(tuned_logistic, metric = "roc_auc")
set.seed(381)
tuned_tree <- tune_grid(
  wf_tree, resamples = folds, grid = grid_tree,
  metrics = metrics_tune, control = control_grid(save_pred = TRUE)
)
show_best(tuned_tree, metric = "roc_auc")
set.seed(381)
tuned_forest <- tune_grid(
  wf_forest, resamples = folds, grid = grid_forest,
  metrics = metrics_tune, control = control_grid(save_pred = TRUE)
)
show_best(tuned_forest, metric = "roc_auc")

Hyper parameters are selected on macro-averaged roc_auc, agreed as the Day-1 placeholder in the work split. Accuracy is reported alongside since the 69.45% majority class makes accuracy alone misleading. Person B’s Task 2 makes the final metric call for model selection; if that differs, only the select_best() calls below need to change.

1.9 Finalise and Fit on Full Training Set

best_logistic <- select_best(tuned_logistic, metric = "roc_auc")
best_tree <- select_best(tuned_tree,     metric = "roc_auc")
best_forest <- select_best(tuned_forest,   metric = "roc_auc")

final_logistic <- finalize_workflow(wf_logistic, best_logistic) %>% fit(data = train)
final_tree <- finalize_workflow(wf_tree, best_tree) %>% fit(data = train)
final_forest <- finalize_workflow(wf_forest, best_forest) %>% fit(data = train)

1.10 Model Parameter Table

param_table <- tibble(
  Technique          = c("Regularised multinomial logistic regression", "Decision tree", "Random forest"),
  Engine = c("glmnet", "rpart", "ranger"),
  Final_Hyperparams = c(sprintf("penalty = %.4g, mixture = %.3f", 
                                best_logistic$penalty, best_logistic$mixture), 
                        sprintf("cost_complexity = %.4g, tree_depth = %d, 
                                min_n = %d", 
                                best_tree$cost_complexity, 
                                best_tree$tree_depth, best_tree$min_n), 
                        sprintf("mtry = %d, min_n = %d, trees = 500", 
                                best_forest$mtry, best_forest$min_n)),
  Resampling = "5-fold CV, stratified on Vulnerability_Tier",
  Seed = 381,
  Optimised_For = "roc_auc (macro, provisional - confirm with Person B)"
)
kable(param_table)

1.11 Predictions Hand-off (Person B)

Both held-out test predictions and cross-validated training-fold predictions are exported, so Person B can compare CV performance against test performance for over fitting.

test_preds <- bind_rows(
  augment(final_logistic, test) %>% mutate(model = "logistic"),
  augment(final_tree, test) %>% mutate(model = "tree"),
  augment(final_forest, test) %>% mutate(model = "forest")
) %>%
  select(HouseholdID, model, Vulnerability_Tier, starts_with(".pred"))

cv_preds <- bind_rows(
  collect_predictions(tuned_logistic, parameters = best_logistic) %>% 
    mutate(model = "logistic"),
  collect_predictions(tuned_tree, parameters = best_tree) %>% 
    mutate(model = "tree"),
  collect_predictions(tuned_forest, parameters = best_forest) %>% 
    mutate(model = "forest")
)

write_csv(test_preds, file.path(OUT_DIR, "test_predictions_for_personB.csv"))
write_csv(cv_preds, file.path(OUT_DIR, "cv_predictions_for_personB.csv"))
write_csv(tier_lookup, file.path(OUT_DIR, "tier_label_lookup.csv"))

print(list.files(OUT_DIR, pattern = "personB|lookup"))
## [1] "cv_predictions_for_personB.csv"   "test_predictions_for_personB.csv"
## [3] "tier_label_lookup.csv"

1.12 Model and Schema Hand-off (Person C)

Person C’s Shiny app needs the fitted models and a schema of what a valid input row looks like, so input validation can be built without guessing column names, types or ranges.

saveRDS(final_logistic, file.path(OUT_DIR, "final_workflow_logistic.rds"))
saveRDS(final_tree,     file.path(OUT_DIR, "final_workflow_tree.rds"))
saveRDS(final_forest,   file.path(OUT_DIR, "final_workflow_forest.rds"))

input_schema <- tibble(
  variable = predictor_vars,
  r_type = c("ordered factor (1-5)", "factor (Urban/Traditional_Tribal/Farms)", 
             "numeric", "numeric (log1p of income)", "numeric (Rand per person)", 
             "factor (Yes/No)", "numeric (count)", "factor (1-12)"),
  valid_range = c("1 to 5; 9 = Unspecified -> reject/flag", "1, 2 or 3 only", 
                  "1 to 25; 0 is invalid -> reject; 8 and 9 ARE valid, do not reject", 
                  "derived from income, not user-entered directly", 
                  "derived from income and household size, not user-entered directly", 
                  "1 or 2; 9 = Unspecified -> reject/flag", 
                  "0 upward; 99 = Unspecified -> reject/flag", 
                  "1 to 12; 99 = Unspecified -> reject/flag"),
  missing_action = "flag and either impute (median/mode, matching the recipes above) or reject per Person C's validation design"
)
write_csv(input_schema, file.path(OUT_DIR, "input_schema_for_personC.csv"))
kable(input_schema)

1.13 Binary Fallback Model (App Interface Fix)

Person C’s app (app/R/score.R) was built against a binary classifier with a single .pred_insecure probability column, before the 3-tier target was finalised as primary. Rather than wait on an app rewrite, a second model is fitted here on Food_Insecure_Binary - already in the data set as the documented fallback target - with its factor levels relabelled so the predicted column lands on exactly .pred_insecure. The app can use this unchanged. The 3-tier models above remain primary for the report and for Person B’s evaluation.

binary_lookup <- tibble(level = c("secure", "insecure"), 
                        label = c("Secure", "Insecure")) 

train_binary <- train %>%   
  mutate(Food_Insecure_Binary = factor(Food_Insecure_Binary,
                                       levels = binary_lookup$label, 
                                       labels = binary_lookup$level)) 

test_binary <- test %>%   
  mutate(Food_Insecure_Binary = factor(Food_Insecure_Binary,
                                       levels = binary_lookup$label, 
                                       labels = binary_lookup$level))
rec_binary <- recipe(Food_Insecure_Binary ~ .,
                     data = train_binary %>% select(-HouseholdID, -Vulnerability_Tier)) %>%
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_other(MainToiletCode, threshold = 0.02) %>%
  step_novel(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

spec_binary <- logistic_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = tune()) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

wf_binary <- workflow() %>% add_recipe(rec_binary) %>% add_model(spec_binary)
set.seed(381)
folds_binary <- vfold_cv(train_binary, v = 5, strata = Food_Insecure_Binary)
grid_binary <- grid_space_filling(penalty(), mixture(), size = 8)

tuned_binary <- tune_grid(
  wf_binary, resamples = folds_binary, grid = grid_binary,
  metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy, bal_accuracy),
  control = control_grid(save_pred = TRUE)
)
show_best(tuned_binary, metric = "roc_auc")
best_binary <- select_best(tuned_binary, metric = "roc_auc")
final_binary <- finalize_workflow(wf_binary, best_binary) %>% fit(data = train_binary)
pred_check <- predict(final_binary, new_data = head(test_binary, 1), type = "prob")
stopifnot(".pred_insecure" %in% names(pred_check))

saveRDS(final_binary, file.path(OUT_DIR, "final_workflow_binary.rds"))
cat("Binary fallback model exported. Columns:", paste(names(pred_check), collapse = ", "), "\n")
## Binary fallback model exported. Columns: .pred_secure, .pred_insecure

Deployed model

The app serves Part A’s binary model (section 1.13). It is copied to models/final_workflow.rds, the file the app and Part B read.

stopifnot(file.copy("data/modelling/final_workflow_binary.rds", "models/final_workflow.rds", overwrite = TRUE))

Part B - Evaluation and Interpretation (Rudi Jan du Plessis)

This notebook covers Task 2 (technical evaluation and model comparison) and Task 3 (interpretation and business evaluation). It starts from Person A’s hand-off in data/modelling/ and does not refit or retune any model. Every number in the Task 2 and Task 3 sections of the report comes from this notebook, and the tables Person C needs (threshold, subgroup performance, monitoring baseline) are written to data/evaluation/.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(glmnet)
library(ranger)
library(rpart)
library(knitr)
tidymodels_prefer()

IN_DIR  <- "data/integrated"
MOD_DIR <- "data/modelling"
OUT_DIR <- "data/evaluation"
dir.create(OUT_DIR, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

set.seed(381)

tiers       <- c("Food_secure", "Food_insecure", "Severely_food_insecure")
tier_labels <- c("Food secure", "Food insecure", "Severely food insecure")
prob_cols   <- paste0(".pred_", tiers)
model_names <- c(logistic = "Multinomial logistic (glmnet)",
                 tree     = "Decision tree (rpart)",
                 forest   = "Random forest (ranger)",
                 binary   = "Binary logistic (glmnet)")
predictor_vars <- c("ComparativeIncomeCode", "GeoTypeCode", "HouseholdSize",
                    "Income_Log", "Income_PerCapita", "ElectricityAccessCode",
                    "SocialGrantRecipients", "MainToiletCode")

2.1 Inputs and Consistency Checks

Person A’s predictions are loaded with HouseholdID as text (the 18-digit IDs lose precision as numbers, DQ-05). Before any metric is computed, the checks below confirm that every model was scored on the same 6,279 test households, that these are exactly the households in M2_test.rds, and that the class mix matches the Milestone 2 split.

read_preds <- function(path) {
  read_csv(path, col_types = cols(HouseholdID = col_character(), id = col_character(),
                                  .default = col_guess())) %>%
    mutate(Vulnerability_Tier = factor(Vulnerability_Tier, levels = tiers),
           .pred_class        = factor(.pred_class, levels = tiers))
}
test_preds <- read_preds(file.path(MOD_DIR, "test_predictions_for_personB.csv"))
cv_preds   <- read_preds(file.path(MOD_DIR, "cv_predictions_for_personB.csv"))

train_raw <- readRDS(file.path(IN_DIR, "M2_train.rds"))
test_raw  <- readRDS(file.path(IN_DIR, "M2_test.rds"))

# Person A's prep_df(), copied unchanged so the binary model sees the same factor coding.
prep_df <- function(df) {
  df %>%
    mutate(
      Vulnerability_Tier    = factor(Vulnerability_Tier, levels = tier_labels, labels = tiers),
      Food_Insecure_Binary  = factor(Food_Insecure_Binary, levels = c("Secure", "Insecure")),
      ComparativeIncomeCode = factor(ComparativeIncomeCode, levels = 1:5, ordered = TRUE),
      GeoTypeCode           = factor(GeoTypeCode, levels = 1:3,
                                     labels = c("Urban", "Traditional_Tribal", "Farms")),
      ElectricityAccessCode = factor(ElectricityAccessCode, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Yes", "No")),
      MainToiletCode        = factor(MainToiletCode)
    ) %>%
    select(HouseholdID, Vulnerability_Tier, Food_Insecure_Binary, all_of(predictor_vars))
}
train <- prep_df(train_raw)
test  <- prep_df(test_raw)

checks <- tibble(
  check = c("Test rows per model",
            "Same households in every model",
            "Prediction households = M2_test households",
            "CV rows per model",
            "Train + test households",
            "Probabilities sum to 1 (max deviation)"),
  result = c(paste(count(test_preds, model)$n, collapse = " / "),
             as.character(n_distinct(test_preds$HouseholdID) == nrow(test)),
             as.character(setequal(test_preds$HouseholdID, as.character(test$HouseholdID))),
             paste(count(cv_preds, model)$n, collapse = " / "),
             format(nrow(train) + nrow(test), big.mark = ","),
             signif(max(abs(rowSums(test_preds[prob_cols]) - 1)), 2))
)
kable(checks)

CV rows per model 14646 / 14646 / 14646
Train + test households 20,925

stopifnot(all(count(test_preds, model)$n == nrow(test)),
          setequal(test_preds$HouseholdID, as.character(test$HouseholdID)),
          nrow(train) + nrow(test) == 20925)

class_mix <- bind_rows(train %>% mutate(set = "Train"), test %>% mutate(set = "Test")) %>%
  count(set, Vulnerability_Tier) %>%
  group_by(set) %>% mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 2)) %>% ungroup()
kable(class_mix)

Binary model predictions

The Shiny app uses Person A’s binary fallback model (final_workflow_binary.rds), not the three-tier models, so it has to be evaluated here too. Person A did not export test predictions for it, so the saved workflow is used to score the same test households. Nothing is refitted.

final_binary <- readRDS(file.path(MOD_DIR, "final_workflow_binary.rds"))

relabel_binary <- function(df) {
  df %>% mutate(Food_Insecure_Binary = factor(Food_Insecure_Binary,
                                              levels = c("Secure", "Insecure"),
                                              labels = c("secure", "insecure")))
}
train_binary <- relabel_binary(train)
test_binary  <- relabel_binary(test)

binary_test_preds <- predict(final_binary, test_binary, type = "prob") %>%
  bind_cols(test_binary %>% select(HouseholdID, Vulnerability_Tier, Food_Insecure_Binary))

# The deployed app file must be this same model, otherwise this evaluation describes the wrong thing.
deployed <- readRDS("models/final_workflow.rds")
same_as_deployed <- isTRUE(all.equal(
  predict(deployed, head(test_binary, 200), type = "prob"),
  predict(final_binary, head(test_binary, 200), type = "prob")))
cat("models/final_workflow.rds gives the same predictions as final_workflow_binary.rds:",
    same_as_deployed, "\n")

2.2 Metric Set and Why

The test set is 69.45% food secure, so a model that labels every household “Food secure” scores 69.45% accuracy and is useless. Accuracy is therefore reported only for reference. The metrics used to compare models are:

Metric Why it is here
Per-class recall (sensitivity) and specificity Shows whether the two food-insecure tiers are being found at all.
Macro-averaged recall (balanced accuracy) and macro F1 Give each tier equal weight, so the 69% majority class cannot carry the score.
Severe-to-secure miss rate Share of severely food-insecure households predicted as food secure: the costliest error, because these households would not be referred.
Hand-Till multiclass ROC-AUC Threshold-free ranking quality across all three tiers, and the metric Person A tuned on.
Macro PR-AUC More informative than ROC-AUC when the positive classes are small (10.55% and 20.00%).
Brier score and calibration plot The app shows a probability to the user, so the probability itself must be trustworthy, not just the ranking.

For screening, the question the app answers is “should this household be referred for follow-up?”. The three-tier output is therefore also collapsed into an at-risk probability, P(Food insecure) + P(Severely food insecure) = 1 - P(Food secure), and evaluated as a binary screen alongside the binary model.

per_class <- function(truth, pred) {
  map_dfr(tiers, function(k) {
    tp <- sum(truth == k & pred == k); fn <- sum(truth == k & pred != k)
    fp <- sum(truth != k & pred == k); tn <- sum(truth != k & pred != k)
    rec  <- tp / (tp + fn)
    prec <- if (tp + fp > 0) tp / (tp + fp) else 0     # a class that is never predicted gets precision 0
    tibble(class = k, n = tp + fn, recall = rec, precision = prec,
           specificity = tn / (tn + fp),
           f1 = if (prec + rec > 0) 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec) else 0)
  })
}

tier_metrics <- function(d) {
  pc <- per_class(d$Vulnerability_Tier, d$.pred_class)
  P  <- as.matrix(d[prob_cols])
  severe <- d$Vulnerability_Tier == "Severely_food_insecure"
  tibble(
    accuracy          = mean(d$Vulnerability_Tier == d$.pred_class),
    macro_recall      = mean(pc$recall),
    macro_f1          = mean(pc$f1),
    recall_secure     = pc$recall[1],
    recall_insecure   = pc$recall[2],
    recall_severe     = pc$recall[3],
    severe_as_secure  = mean(d$.pred_class[severe] == "Food_secure"),
    roc_auc_hand_till = roc_auc_vec(d$Vulnerability_Tier, P, estimator = "hand_till"),
    pr_auc_macro      = pr_auc_vec(d$Vulnerability_Tier, P, estimator = "macro"),
    brier             = brier_class_vec(d$Vulnerability_Tier, P)
  )
}

# Binary screen: truth = at risk (any food insecurity), score = probability of being at risk.
risk_factor <- function(x) factor(ifelse(x, "at_risk", "secure"), levels = c("at_risk", "secure"))

screen_metrics <- function(at_risk, p, threshold) {
  flag <- p >= threshold
  tp <- sum(flag & at_risk); fn <- sum(!flag & at_risk); fp <- sum(flag & !at_risk); tn <- sum(!flag & !at_risk)
  rec <- tp / (tp + fn); prec <- if (tp + fp > 0) tp / (tp + fp) else 0
  tibble(threshold   = threshold,
         recall      = rec,
         precision   = prec,
         specificity = tn / (tn + fp),
         f1          = if (prec + rec > 0) 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec) else 0,
         f2          = if (prec + rec > 0) 5 * prec * rec / (4 * prec + rec) else 0,
         pct_flagged = mean(flag))
}

screen_auc <- function(at_risk, p) {
  tibble(roc_auc = roc_auc_vec(risk_factor(at_risk), p),
         pr_auc  = pr_auc_vec(risk_factor(at_risk), p),
         brier   = mean((p - at_risk)^2))
}

The CV-vs-test comparison above shows whether the tuned settings generalise. The training-set fit below shows how much each final model memorised: a large gap between training and test AUC means the model learned noise.

)

Bootstrap confidence intervals on the test set

The test set is resampled 1,000 times with replacement. The same resamples are used for every model, so the difference between two models can be given its own interval. If that interval contains 0, the test set cannot tell the two models apart.

set.seed(381)
B <- 1000
wide <- test_preds %>%
  select(HouseholdID, model, Vulnerability_Tier, .pred_class, all_of(prob_cols)) %>%
  arrange(model, HouseholdID)
by_model <- split(wide, wide$model)
n_test <- nrow(test)
boot_idx <- replicate(B, sample.int(n_test, n_test, replace = TRUE), simplify = FALSE)

boot_one <- function(d, idx) {
  d <- d[idx, ]
  pc <- per_class(d$Vulnerability_Tier, d$.pred_class)
  c(auc = roc_auc_vec(d$Vulnerability_Tier, as.matrix(d[prob_cols]), estimator = "hand_till"),
    macro_recall = mean(pc$recall))
}
boot_res <- imap_dfr(by_model, function(d, m) {
  map_dfr(seq_len(B), function(b) as_tibble_row(c(model = m, b = b, boot_one(d, boot_idx[[b]]))))
}) %>% mutate(across(c(b, auc, macro_recall), as.numeric))

boot_ci <- boot_res %>%
  pivot_longer(c(auc, macro_recall), names_to = "metric") %>%
  group_by(model, metric) %>%
  summarise(estimate_mean = mean(value),
            ci_low = quantile(value, 0.025), ci_high = quantile(value, 0.975), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(model = model_names[model])

2.5 Decision Threshold

Assigning each household to its highest-probability tier hides the food-insecure households. The probability of “Food secure” starts at around 0.69 for a typical household, so the minority tiers rarely win. For screening, the app instead compares the at-risk probability with a referral threshold.

The threshold is chosen on the cross-validation predictions (training folds only), never on the test set, so the test result stays an honest estimate.

Two rules were compared:

  • F2-optimal: weights recall twice as heavily as precision, the usual choice when a miss costs more than a false alarm.
  • 80% recall at the fewest referrals: the highest threshold that still finds at least 80% of at-risk households in cross-validation.

Both reflect that missing a food-insecure household costs more than a false alarm. The household is not followed up, while a false alarm costs one review by an official. The deciding factor is workload. Business Objective 2 is about targeting limited resources, and a screen that refers almost every household does not prioritise anything. The 80% recall rule is used, and the F2 result is reported to show why it was rejected.

# Out-of-fold predictions for the binary model, from its own 5 folds (same seed and strata as Person A).
set.seed(381)
folds_binary <- vfold_cv(train_binary, v = 5, strata = Food_Insecure_Binary)
wf_binary_unfitted <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(extract_preprocessor(final_binary)) %>%
  add_model(extract_spec_parsnip(final_binary))
cv_binary <- fit_resamples(wf_binary_unfitted, folds_binary,
                           control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE))
cv_binary_preds <- collect_predictions(cv_binary)
cv_binary_auc <- collect_metrics(cv_binary, summarize = FALSE) %>%
  filter(.metric == "roc_auc") %>%
  summarise(cv_mean = mean(.estimate), cv_sd = sd(.estimate))

cv_screen <- bind_rows(
  cv_preds %>% transmute(model, at_risk = Vulnerability_Tier != "Food_secure", p = 1 - .pred_Food_secure),
  cv_binary_preds %>% transmute(model = "binary", at_risk = Food_Insecure_Binary == "insecure", p = .pred_insecure)
)
grid <- seq(0.05, 0.80, by = 0.01)
threshold_curves <- cv_screen %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  group_modify(~ map_dfr(grid, function(t) screen_metrics(.x$at_risk, .x$p, t))) %>%
  ungroup()

chosen <- threshold_curves %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  summarise(threshold_f2 = threshold[which.max(f2)],
            threshold_recall80 = max(threshold[recall >= 0.80]))
kable(chosen, caption = "Thresholds chosen on cross-validation predictions")

2.6 Calibration

calib <- screen_scores %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  mutate(bin = ntile(p, 10)) %>%
  group_by(model, bin) %>%
  summarise(mean_pred = mean(p), observed = mean(at_risk), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

ece <- calib %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  summarise(ece = sum(n * abs(mean_pred - observed)) / sum(n)) %>%
  mutate(model = model_names[model])
write_csv(left_join(screen_test_auc %>% select(model, brier), ece, by = "model"), file.path(OUT_DIR, "calibration.csv"))

2.7 Evaluation Matrix and Final Model Selection

time_fit <- function(wf, data) {
  spec <- workflow() %>% add_recipe(extract_preprocessor(wf)) %>% add_model(extract_spec_parsnip(wf))
  set.seed(381)
  unname(system.time(fit(spec, data))["elapsed"])
}
train_seconds <- c(
  logistic = time_fit(final_wf$logistic, train %>% select(-HouseholdID, -Food_Insecure_Binary)),
  tree     = time_fit(final_wf$tree,     train %>% select(-HouseholdID, -Food_Insecure_Binary)),
  forest   = time_fit(final_wf$forest,   train %>% select(-HouseholdID, -Food_Insecure_Binary)),
  binary   = time_fit(final_binary,      train_binary %>% select(-HouseholdID, -Vulnerability_Tier))
)
kable(enframe(train_seconds, "model", "seconds_to_fit"), digits = 1)
model seconds_to_fit
logistic 0.7
tree 0.4
forest 6.9
binary 0.4

The matrix brings together the evidence from 2.3 to 2.6 with the non-statistical criteria. All four models are compared on the screening task, because that is the decision the app supports and the only measure on which the binary model and the three-tier models can be compared directly. Each criterion is scored from 5 (best) down to a floor of 1. A model loses points for its distance from the best model, at a fixed rate per criterion, so a difference too small to matter costs almost nothing:

Criterion Evidence Points lost
Discrimination Test screening ROC-AUC 1 per 0.01 below the best
Referral efficiency Precision at the chosen threshold (share of referred households that are really at risk) 1 per 0.01 below the best
Calibration Test Brier score of the at-risk probability 1 per 0.005 above the best
Robustness Gap between CV and test screening AUC, plus the fold-to-fold SD 1 per 0.005 above the best
Interpretability Judgement: can an official see why a household was flagged? 5 = one odds ratio per factor, 4 = readable but more complex (per-tier coefficients, or a depth-11 tree), 2 = black box that needs post-hoc explanation
Deployment fit Judgement: does it match the app (one at-risk probability, fast to score, small file)? 5 = built for the app’s interface, 3 = needs the app changed to collapse three tiers

The training-vs-test gap from 2.4 is shown as evidence but not scored. A random forest always fits its own training data almost perfectly, so that gap overstates its overfitting, while its CV-vs-test gap is small.

cv_screen_folds <- bind_rows(
  cv_preds %>% transmute(model, id, at_risk = Vulnerability_Tier != "Food_secure", p = 1 - .pred_Food_secure),
  cv_binary_preds %>% transmute(model = "binary", id, at_risk = Food_Insecure_Binary == "insecure", p = .pred_insecure)
) %>%
  group_by(model, id) %>%
  summarise(auc = roc_auc_vec(risk_factor(at_risk), p), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  summarise(cv_screen_auc = mean(auc), cv_screen_auc_sd = sd(auc))

matrix_raw <- tibble(model = c("logistic", "tree", "forest", "binary")) %>%
  left_join(cv_summary %>% filter(metric == "roc_auc_hand_till") %>% select(model, cv_auc_3tier = cv_mean), by = "model") %>%
  left_join(test_preds %>% group_by(model) %>% group_modify(~ tier_metrics(.x)) %>% ungroup() %>%
              select(model, test_auc_3tier = roc_auc_hand_till, macro_recall, recall_insecure_tier = recall_insecure), by = "model") %>%
  left_join(cv_screen_folds, by = "model") %>%
  left_join(screen_scores %>% group_by(model) %>% group_modify(~ screen_auc(.x$at_risk, .x$p)) %>% ungroup() %>%
              select(model, screen_auc = roc_auc, screen_pr_auc = pr_auc, screen_brier = brier), by = "model") %>%
  left_join(calib %>% group_by(model) %>% summarise(ece = sum(n * abs(mean_pred - observed)) / sum(n)), by = "model") %>%
  left_join(screen_test_at_threshold %>% filter(str_detect(rule, "chosen")) %>%
              transmute(model = names(model_names)[match(model, model_names)], threshold, screen_recall = recall,
                        screen_precision = precision, pct_flagged), by = "model") %>%
  left_join(train_fit %>% transmute(model = names(model_names)[match(model, model_names)], train_test_gap = gap), by = "model") %>%
  mutate(cv_test_gap = abs(screen_auc - cv_screen_auc),
         train_seconds = train_seconds[model],
         interpretability = c(logistic = 4, tree = 4, forest = 2, binary = 5)[model],
         deployment_fit   = c(logistic = 3, tree = 3, forest = 3, binary = 5)[model])

points <- function(x, per_point, higher_is_better = TRUE) {
  gap <- if (higher_is_better) max(x) - x else x - min(x)
  round(pmax(1, 5 - gap / per_point), 1)
}

weights <- c(discrimination = 0.25, efficiency = 0.15, calibration = 0.15,
             robustness = 0.10, interpretability = 0.20, deployment_fit = 0.15)

eval_matrix <- matrix_raw %>%
  mutate(
    s_discrimination   = points(screen_auc, 0.01),
    s_efficiency       = points(screen_precision, 0.01),
    s_calibration      = points(screen_brier, 0.005, higher_is_better = FALSE),
    s_robustness       = points(cv_test_gap + cv_screen_auc_sd, 0.005, higher_is_better = FALSE),
    s_interpretability = interpretability,
    s_deployment_fit   = deployment_fit,
    weighted_score = round(weights["discrimination"] * s_discrimination +
                           weights["efficiency"] * s_efficiency +
                           weights["calibration"] * s_calibration +
                           weights["robustness"] * s_robustness +
                           weights["interpretability"] * s_interpretability +
                           weights["deployment_fit"] * s_deployment_fit, 2),
    model = model_names[model]
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(weighted_score))

kable(eval_matrix %>% select(model, cv_auc_3tier, test_auc_3tier, macro_recall, recall_insecure_tier,
                             cv_screen_auc, cv_screen_auc_sd, screen_auc, screen_pr_auc, threshold,
                             screen_recall, screen_precision, pct_flagged, screen_brier, ece,
                             train_test_gap, train_seconds),
      digits = 3, caption = "Evaluation matrix - evidence (test set unless marked CV; three-tier columns are blank for the binary model)")

3.1 Drivers of Food Insecurity

Observed rates

Before any model, the share of households with any food insecurity at each level of the hypothesis variables, on the full modelling set. These are raw associations: they do not adjust for income or anything else.

full <- bind_rows(train_binary, test_binary)
rate_by <- function(data = full, var) {
  data %>%
    filter(!is.na(.data[[var]])) %>%
    mutate(level = as.character(.data[[var]])) %>%
    group_by(variable = var, level) %>%
    summarise(households = n(), pct_food_insecure = round(100 * mean(Food_Insecure_Binary == "insecure"), 1),
              .groups = "drop")
}

)

Odds ratios

The odds ratios below come from an unpenalised binary logistic regression (any food insecurity vs food secure) fitted on the training set. Person A’s tuned penalty was effectively zero (8.1e-10), so the penalised and unpenalised coefficients are practically the same, and the unpenalised fit adds standard errors and confidence intervals. Income_PerCapita is left out of this model on purpose. Total income and household size are both already in the model, and per-capita income is their ratio, so keeping it would make the household-size coefficient meaningless (H3 asks about household size at a fixed total income).

or_data <- train_binary %>%
  mutate(ComparativeIncomeCode = factor(ComparativeIncomeCode, ordered = FALSE),
         MainToiletCode = fct_lump_prop(MainToiletCode, 0.02, other_level = "Other"))

or_model <- glm(Food_Insecure_Binary ~ ComparativeIncomeCode + GeoTypeCode + HouseholdSize +
                  Income_Log + ElectricityAccessCode + SocialGrantRecipients + MainToiletCode,
                data = or_data, family = binomial())

  mutate(across(c(estimate, conf.low, conf.high), ~ round(.x, 3)),
         p.value = signif(p.value, 3))

Permutation importance

Each predictor is shuffled on the test set (5 repeats), and the drop in ROC-AUC is recorded. A large drop means the model relies on that predictor. This is model-agnostic, so the same yardstick applies to the logistic models and the forest.

perm_importance <- function(predict_fun, data, truth, score_fun, vars, reps = 5) {
  base <- score_fun(truth, predict_fun(data))
  map_dfr(vars, function(v) {
    drops <- map_dbl(seq_len(reps), function(r) {
      shuffled <- data
      shuffled[[v]] <- sample(shuffled[[v]])
      base - score_fun(truth, predict_fun(shuffled))
    })
    tibble(variable = v, auc_drop = mean(drops), auc_drop_sd = sd(drops))
  })
}
auc3 <- function(truth, P) roc_auc_vec(truth, as.matrix(P[prob_cols]), estimator = "hand_till")
auc2 <- function(truth, p) roc_auc_vec(truth, p$.pred_secure)

set.seed(381)
importance <- bind_rows(
  perm_importance(function(d) predict(final_wf$logistic, d, type = "prob"), test,
                  test$Vulnerability_Tier, auc3, predictor_vars) %>% mutate(model = "logistic"),
  perm_importance(function(d) predict(final_wf$forest, d, type = "prob"), test,
                  test$Vulnerability_Tier, auc3, predictor_vars) %>% mutate(model = "forest"),
  perm_importance(function(d) predict(final_binary, d, type = "prob"), test_binary,
                  test_binary$Food_Insecure_Binary, auc2, predictor_vars) %>% mutate(model = "binary")
) %>%
  group_by(model) %>% mutate(rank = rank(-auc_drop)) %>% ungroup()
write_csv(importance, file.path(OUT_DIR, "permutation_importance.csv"))

importance %>%
  mutate(model = model_names[model]) %>%
  ggplot(aes(auc_drop, reorder(variable, auc_drop))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2171b5") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = auc_drop - auc_drop_sd, xmax = auc_drop + auc_drop_sd), height = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(x = "Drop in test ROC-AUC when the predictor is shuffled", y = NULL,
       title = "Permutation importance (higher = the model leans on it more)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

Partial dependence

The partial-dependence plots show how the average at-risk probability changes as one predictor is varied, with the other predictors held at their observed values. Income and household size are varied together with Income_PerCapita, so the model never sees an impossible combination such as a high income with a low per-capita income for a one-person household.

set.seed(381)
pd_base <- train_binary %>% slice_sample(n = 1500)

at_risk_prob <- list(
  binary   = function(d) predict(final_binary, d, type = "prob")$.pred_insecure,
  logistic = function(d) 1 - predict(final_wf$logistic, d, type = "prob")$.pred_Food_secure,
  forest   = function(d) 1 - predict(final_wf$forest, d, type = "prob")$.pred_Food_secure
)

pd_set <- function(d, var, value) {
  if (var == "Income_Log") {
    d$Income_Log <- value
    d$Income_PerCapita <- expm1(value) / d$HouseholdSize
  } else if (var == "HouseholdSize") {
    d$Income_PerCapita <- expm1(d$Income_Log) / value
    d$HouseholdSize <- value
  } else if (is.factor(d[[var]])) {
    d[[var]] <- factor(value, levels = levels(d[[var]]), ordered = is.ordered(d[[var]]))
  } else {
    d[[var]] <- value
  }
  d
}

pd_grid <- list(
  Income_Log            = unique(log1p(round(expm1(quantile(train$Income_Log, seq(0.05, 0.95, 0.05), na.rm = TRUE)), -2))),
  HouseholdSize         = 1:10,
  SocialGrantRecipients = 0:6,
  GeoTypeCode           = levels(train$GeoTypeCode),
  ElectricityAccessCode = levels(train$ElectricityAccessCode),
  ComparativeIncomeCode = levels(train$ComparativeIncomeCode),
  MainToiletCode        = names(which(table(train$MainToiletCode) / nrow(train) >= 0.02))
)

pdp <- imap_dfr(at_risk_prob, function(f, m) {
  imap_dfr(pd_grid, function(values, var) {
    map_dfr(values, function(v) tibble(model = m, variable = var, value = as.character(v),
                                       x_num = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(v)),
                                       at_risk = mean(f(pd_set(pd_base, var, v)), na.rm = TRUE)))
  })
})
write_csv(pdp, file.path(OUT_DIR, "partial_dependence.csv"))

pdp %>%
  mutate(model = model_names[model],
         label = ifelse(variable == "Income_Log",
                        sprintf("R%s", format(round(expm1(x_num), -2), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)), value),
         x = paste0(label, "___", variable)) %>%   # unique per facet, so each facet keeps its own order
  group_by(variable) %>% mutate(step = match(value, unique(value))) %>% ungroup() %>%
  arrange(variable, step) %>%
  mutate(x = fct_inorder(x)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x, at_risk, colour = model, group = model)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = function(l) sub("___.*", "", l)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average at-risk probability", colour = NULL,
       title = "Partial dependence (income shown as monthly Rand)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 6), legend.position = "bottom")

3.2 Subgroup Performance

Recall, false-negative rate and precision for the final screening model at its chosen threshold, by settlement type, income band, household-size band, grant receipt and province. The bands match R/fairness_check.R so that Person C’s fairness section and this table use the same groups. The intervals are 95% Wilson intervals: a wide interval means the group is too small to judge.

FINAL_MODEL <- "binary"   # confirmed in the evaluation matrix above; see the report for the reasoning
FINAL_THRESHOLD <- chosen$threshold_recall80[chosen$model == FINAL_MODEL]

integrated <- readRDS(file.path(IN_DIR, "household_integrated.rds")) %>%
  transmute(HouseholdID = as.character(HouseholdID), ProvinceCode, HouseholdWeight)
province_names <- c("Western Cape", "Eastern Cape", "Northern Cape", "Free State", "KwaZulu-Natal",
                    "North West", "Gauteng", "Mpumalanga", "Limpopo")

final_test <- screen_scores %>%
  filter(model == FINAL_MODEL) %>%
  left_join(test %>% mutate(HouseholdID = as.character(HouseholdID)) %>%
              select(HouseholdID, Vulnerability_Tier, all_of(predictor_vars)), by = "HouseholdID") %>%
  left_join(integrated, by = "HouseholdID") %>%
  mutate(flag = p >= FINAL_THRESHOLD,
         income = expm1(Income_Log),
         income_band = cut(income, c(-Inf, 2500, 5000, 11500, Inf),
                           labels = c("< R2,500", "R2,500-5,000", "R5,000-11,500", "> R11,500")),
         size_band  = cut(HouseholdSize, c(0, 2, 4, 6, Inf), labels = c("1-2", "3-4", "5-6", "7+")),
         grant_band = ifelse(SocialGrantRecipients > 0, "Receives grants", "No grants"),
         province   = province_names[ProvinceCode])
stopifnot(sum(is.na(final_test$ProvinceCode)) == 0)

subgroup_row <- function(d) {
  tp <- sum(d$flag & d$at_risk); fn <- sum(!d$flag & d$at_risk); fp <- sum(d$flag & !d$at_risk)
  ci <- if (tp + fn > 0) suppressWarnings(prop.test(tp, tp + fn, correct = FALSE)$conf.int) else c(NA, NA)
  tibble(households = nrow(d), at_risk = tp + fn,
         recall = tp / (tp + fn), recall_95_low = ci[1], recall_95_high = ci[2],
         false_negative_rate = fn / (tp + fn),
         precision = if (tp + fp > 0) tp / (tp + fp) else NA_real_,
         pct_flagged = mean(d$flag))
}
overall <- subgroup_row(final_test)

subgroups <- map_dfr(c(GeoTypeCode = "GeoTypeCode", income_band = "income_band", size_band = "size_band",
                       grant_band = "grant_band", province = "province"),
                     function(g) final_test %>% filter(!is.na(.data[[g]])) %>%
                       group_by(group = as.character(.data[[g]])) %>%
                       group_modify(~ subgroup_row(.x)) %>% ungroup() %>% mutate(variable = g)) %>%
  mutate(gap_vs_overall = recall - overall$recall,
         within_10_points = abs(gap_vs_overall) <= 0.10) %>%
  relocate(variable)

kable(overall, digits = 3, caption = sprintf("Overall test performance, %s at threshold %.2f",
                                              model_names[FINAL_MODEL], FINAL_THRESHOLD))

  summarise(unweighted_at_risk_rate = mean(at_risk),

            weighted_recall         = sum(HouseholdWeight * (flag & at_risk)) / sum(HouseholdWeight * at_risk))

Part C - Deployment, Monitoring and Ethics (Timothy Wubbeling)

This notebook covers Task 4 (deployment and monitoring) and the ethics and fairness part of Task 3. It starts from Person A’s final workflow (models/final_workflow.rds) and Person B’s evaluation outputs (data/evaluation/), and does not refit any model. It is the evidence behind the deployment, monitoring and fairness sections of the report: the validation path for new data, proof that the Shiny app reproduces the evaluated model exactly, the explanation method, the fairness check, and the monitoring baselines and drift test.

library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(workflows)
source("app/R/validate.R")    # validate_households(), read_upload(), RULES
source("app/R/score.R")       # to_model_input(), score_households()
source("app/R/monitor.R")     # psi(), batch_summary()
source("R/fairness_check.R")  # subgroup_table(), add_bands()

4.1 Deployed Model and Threshold

The app must serve exactly the model Person B evaluated, at the threshold Person B chose. Both are checked here rather than assumed.

wf       <- readRDS("models/final_workflow.rds")
ref      <- readRDS("models/reference.rds")
baseline <- read.csv("data/evaluation/monitoring_baseline.csv")
THRESHOLD <- baseline$threshold

same_file <- unname(tools::md5sum("models/final_workflow.rds")) ==
             unname(tools::md5sum("data/modelling/final_workflow_binary.rds"))
app_line  <- grep("^THRESHOLD", readLines("app/app.R"), value = TRUE)
app_threshold <- as.numeric(sub("^THRESHOLD *<- *([0-9.]+).*", "\\1", app_line))
stopifnot(same_file, app_threshold == THRESHOLD)

cat("Deployed model is Person A's binary workflow:", same_file,
    "| app threshold:", app_threshold, "| reference version:", ref$model_version, "\n")

4.2 Path for New Data: Validate, Clean, Preprocess, Score

New households enter through the single-household form or a CSV upload, and both go through the same four steps:

  1. Validate (app/R/validate.R): the seven inputs must be present; every column is read as text so 18-digit HouseholdIDs stay exact (the Milestone 2 precision defect); food-insecurity items in an upload are ignored (leakage rule); duplicate IDs are flagged.
  2. Clean: the Milestone 2 rules, column by column (table below). Sentinels and text tokens become missing; unseen codes, impossible values and rows with more than two missing inputs are not scored.
  3. Preprocess (to_model_input() in app/R/score.R): raw codes become the model’s features exactly as in Person A’s prep_df() (labelled factors, Income_Log = log1p(income), Income_PerCapita = income / household size); the workflow’s recipe then imputes, encodes and scales with values learned on the training data only.
  4. Score: the probability of food insecurity, “Higher risk: refer for review” at or above the threshold, and the three inputs that move the probability most.
fmt <- function(x) format(x, scientific = FALSE, big.mark = " ", trim = TRUE)
rules_tbl <- data.frame(
  input = names(RULES),
  recoded_to_missing = sapply(RULES, function(r) if (length(r$sentinels)) paste(fmt(r$sentinels), collapse = ", ") else "-"),
  valid = sapply(RULES, function(r) if (!is.null(r$levels)) paste0("codes ", min(r$levels), "-", max(r$levels))
                                     else paste0(fmt(r$min), " to ", fmt(r$max), " (above: warning)")),
  row.names = NULL)
kable(rules_tbl, caption = "Per-input cleaning rules (from the Milestone 2 sentinel map)")
Per-input cleaning rules (from the Milestone 2 sentinel map)

4.4 Explaining a Result

For each household, each input in turn is swapped for the typical training value (median for counts and income, most common code for categories) and the household is re-scored; the change in probability is that input’s contribution. The three largest are shown. This works for any model type, but it changes one input at a time (no interactions), depends on the chosen baseline, and shows association, not cause.

examples <- data.frame(
  ComparativeIncomeCode = c(5, 2), GeoTypeCode = c(2, 1), HouseholdSize = c(6, 2),
  TotalMonthlyHouseholdIncomeRaw = c(1200, 30000), ElectricityAccessCode = c(2, 1),
  SocialGrantRecipients = c(2, 0), MainToiletCode = c(5, 1))
ex <- score_households(wf, validate_households(examples), ref, THRESHOLD)
kable(cbind(household = c("Rural, income fell, no electricity", "Urban, R30 000 a month"),
            ex[, c("probability", "predicted", "main_factors")]),
      caption = "Two example households scored by the app")

4.5 Fairness: Equal Opportunity

Criterion: among households that really are food insecure, the screen should find a similar share in every group (similar recall, i.e. similar false-negative rate), because a missed food-insecure household is the costliest error. The tolerance was set before the results were examined: a group’s recall within 10 percentage points of overall recall. Recall is shown with 95% Wilson intervals because some groups are small.

The same table is recomputed independently with R/fairness_check.R from Person B’s test predictions, as a check that both use the same groups and the same definition.

preds <- add_bands(read.csv("data/evaluation/final_model_test_predictions.csv"))
mine  <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("GeoTypeCode", "income_band", "size_band", "grant_band"),
                               function(g) subgroup_table(preds, g, THRESHOLD)))
both  <- merge(mine[, c("variable", "group", "households", "insecure", "recall")],
               sub[, c("variable", "group", "households", "at_risk", "recall")],
               by = c("variable", "group"), suffixes = c("_personC", "_personB"))
# fairness_check.R rounds recall to 3 decimals; compare at that precision, and the counts exactly
stopifnot(nrow(both) == nrow(mine),
          all(both$households_personC == both$households_personB),
          all(both$insecure == both$at_risk),
          max(abs(both$recall_personC - round(both$recall_personB, 3))) < 1e-9)
cat("Recomputed for", nrow(both), "groups: same households, same at-risk counts, same recall as Person B.\n")
## Recomputed for 13 groups: same households, same at-risk counts, same recall as Person B.
kable(sub %>% filter(!within_10_points) %>%
        select(variable, group, households, at_risk, recall, recall_95_low, recall_95_high, gap_vs_overall),
      digits = 3, caption = "Groups outside the 10-point tolerance")

Settlement type and all nine provinces are within tolerance; farm households (197 in the test set, 62 at risk) have a wide interval, so no claim of parity is made for them. Four groups fall outside. The screen catches more of the at-risk households among the poorest and the largest households, and far fewer among households with incomes above R11,500 a month and households with no grant recipients: food-insecure households that do not look poor on these inputs are the ones the model misses. These findings are carried into the ethics register and the usage limits shown in the app.

4.6 Monitoring: Baselines and a Drift Test

The outcome is only observed when Stats SA releases a new GHS, so between releases the app monitors its inputs and outputs. Each upload writes one row of totals (no household rows) to monitoring/batch_log.csv. Here the same summary is computed for two batches: 1 000 randomly chosen test households as they are, and the same households with a simulated shift (incomes 25% higher, as after about five years of inflation, and a third of urban households recorded as traditional/tribal).

test <- readRDS("data/integrated/M2_test.rds")
score_batch <- function(df) score_households(wf, validate_households(df[PREDICTORS]), ref, THRESHOLD)

set.seed(381)
as_is   <- test[sample(nrow(test), 1000), ]   # random, so the batch reflects the whole test set
shifted <- as_is
shifted$TotalMonthlyHouseholdIncomeRaw <- shifted$TotalMonthlyHouseholdIncomeRaw * 1.25
urban <- which(shifted$GeoTypeCode == 1)
shifted$GeoTypeCode[sample(urban, round(length(urban) / 3))] <- 2

batches <- rbind(cbind(batch = "Test households as they are", batch_summary(score_batch(as_is), ref, THRESHOLD)),
                 cbind(batch = "Simulated shift",             batch_summary(score_batch(shifted), ref, THRESHOLD)))

# Alert rules from the monitoring plan (as in R/review_monitoring.R)
worst <- pmax(batches$psi_income, batches$psi_geotype, batches$psi_hhsize, na.rm = TRUE)
batches$drift <- ifelse(worst > 0.25, "ACT: significant shift", ifelse(worst > 0.10, "watch", "stable"))
batches$output_shift <- ifelse(abs(batches$pct_higher_risk - 100 * baseline$test_pct_flagged) > 10,
                               "check threshold and drift", "ok")
kable(batches[, c("batch", "rows", "pct_not_scored", "pct_income_missing", "psi_income",
                  "psi_geotype", "psi_hhsize", "pct_higher_risk", "drift", "output_shift")],
      digits = 3, caption = "Monitoring summary per batch, with the alert rules applied")

plan <- data.frame(
  signal   = c("Input drift (income, settlement type, household size)", "Missing income",
               "Rows not scored", "Share flagged higher risk", "Recall (at each GHS release)",
               "Calibration (at each GHS release)", "Subgroup recall (at each GHS release)"),
  baseline = c("PSI 0", "2.2% (451 of 20 940 in M2)", "0% of test rows",
               sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * baseline$test_pct_flagged), sprintf("%.3f", baseline$test_recall),
               sprintf("Brier %.3f", baseline$test_brier), "Person B's subgroup table"),
  alert    = c("PSI 0.10-0.25 watch; above 0.25 act", "above 5%", "above 5%", "+/- 10 points",
               sprintf("below %.3f", baseline$recall_alert_below), "Brier clearly worse", "gap above 10 points"))
kable(plan, caption = "Monitoring thresholds tied to the test-set baseline")
